hints: Start by comparing each row in Table 7.1 with the resting potentials given in the text, -50 mV for the chemoreceptor and -70 mV for the dendrite.
Think about what a stimulus must do to a receptor cell membrane to move it away from resting potential, and what happens if the stimulus is too weak.
Link the two cells together - how does a change in the chemoreceptor lead to a change in the dendrite across the synapse in Fig. 7.1?
Focus on why 1.0 and 10.0 $\text{g dm}^{-3}$ give exactly the same potentials, +30 mV and +40 mV, even though concentration increases ten-fold.
walkthrough:
Reading the low concentration result**
At 0.1 $\text{g dm}^{-3}$ the chemoreceptor is at -50 mV, which is exactly its resting potential, and the dendrite is at -70 mV, exactly its resting potential. That tells you the salt stimulus was too weak to open ion channels in the microvilli membrane, so no $\text{Na}^{+}$ influx occurred, no depolarisation and no generator / receptor potential large enough to matter.

No synaptic communication when below threshold**
Because the chemoreceptor stays polarised, voltage-gated $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ channels at its base stay closed and no neurotransmitter is released into the synapse. Without transmitter binding to the dendrite membrane, ligand-gated $\text{Na}^{+}$ channels stay closed, so the dendrite stays at -70 mV with no action potential.

Explaining the higher concentration results**
At 1.0 $\text{g dm}^{-3}$ the chemoreceptor jumps to +30 mV. $\text{Na}^{+}$ entry has depolarised it fully. That depolarisation triggers neurotransmitter release, which depolarises the dendrite membrane to threshold and fires an action potential to +40 mV. This is the causal chain: stimulus -> receptor depolarisation -> transmitter -> sensory depolarisation.

Why stronger stimulus gives no bigger response**
10.0 $\text{g dm}^{-3}$ gives the same +30 mV and +40 mV. Once threshold is reached, the response is maximal. Action potentials and receptor depolarisation follow the all-or-nothing law, so increasing stimulus intensity beyond threshold does not increase the size of the potential.

Final answer: At 0.1 $\text{g dm}^{-3}$ the chemoreceptor remains at resting potential, -50 mV, so is not depolarised and does not release neurotransmitter, so the dendrite remains at resting potential, -70 mV, with no action potential. At 1.0 and 10.0 $\text{g dm}^{-3}$ the chemoreceptor is depolarised to +30 mV and releases neurotransmitter, triggering depolarisation / action potential to +40 mV in the dendrite. Identical responses at 1.0 and 10.0 $\text{g dm}^{-3}$ show threshold has been exceeded and the all-or-nothing law.

hints: Picture where each neurone sits in a reflex arc - one connects receptor to CNS, the other connects CNS to muscle or gland.
Recall the distinctive shape of a sensory neurone with its cell body off to one side, compared with the large cell body with many short branches in a motor neurone.
Think about pairing one structural difference with its functional difference to make a clear contrast for each mark.
walkthrough:
Cell body position**
In a sensory neurone the cell body sits in the middle of the fibre, between a dendron on the receptor side and the axon on the CNS side, often in a dorsal root ganglion outside the cord. In a motor neurone the cell body is at one end of the cell, inside the CNS in brain or spinal cord, with the long axon running out to the effector.

Processes leaving the cell body**
A sensory neurone has no true dendrites sprouting from the cell body itself. It has one dendron bringing impulses in and one axon taking them on, both myelinated and often long. A motor neurone has many short branched dendrites extending directly from the cell body to collect synaptic inputs, plus a single very long axon to carry the output.

Opposite functions**
Function follows that wiring. Sensory neurones carry impulses from a receptor toward the CNS or to an intermediate neurone. Motor neurones carry impulses away from the CNS or intermediate neurone outward to an effector such as muscle or gland.

Final answer: Sensory neurone has cell body between dendron and axon / in dorsal root ganglion, motor neurone has cell body at end / in CNS; sensory has dendron and long axon with no dendrites on cell body, motor has many dendrites extending from cell body and long axon; sensory carries impulses from receptor to CNS / intermediate neurone, motor carries impulses from CNS / intermediate neurone to effector.
